title: Urban Form and Wayfinding: Review of Cognitive and Spatial Knowledge for Individuals' Navigation
authors: Vaez, S, Burke, M, Alizadeh, T, 2016
review_question: To provide an up-to-date understanding of how theory drawn from different fields of research may explain how people perceive the urban environment and find their way in and through it.
inclusion_exclusion_criteria: Studies of human spatial cognition and wayfinding from 1960 till the present, identified using prescribed terms.

findings.antecedent: Urban elements (paths, edges, nodes, districts, landmarks)
findings.quote: Lynch (1960, p. 3) described a legible city as one whose urban components - paths, districts and landmarks – “are easily identifiable and are easily grouped into an over-all pattern”

findings.antecedent: Environmental variables (visual access, differentiation, layout configuration, signage)
findings.quote: Weisman (1981) built on these understandings, identifying four environmental variables that influence an individuals' wayfinding behaviour

findings.antecedent: Imageable features of urban environment (unique, unusual buildings, distinct elements)
findings.consequent: Stronger mental image and memorability for observers
findings.quote: Imageability is the visual aspect of an urban environment, which helps an observer generate an image of his surrounding environment and create meaning of it.

findings.antecedent: High integration value (of street lines) in urban network
findings.source: 4.3 Urban Configurational Features and Wayfinding Behaviour: Space syntax
findings.quote: Hillier (1985) made a comparison of syntactic values of spatial configuration and the number of pedestrian movements along street lines, finding a strong positive correlation between integration value and density of movement.

findings.consequent: Route choice and cognitive map formation
findings.source: 4.3 Urban Configurational Features and Wayfinding Behaviour: Space syntax
findings.quote: Haq (1999a, 1999b, 2003) and Haq & Zimring (2001) found the important role of connectivity in choosing routes during wayfinding process and cognitive map formation.

findings.consequent: Better cognitive maps (more representative of environment)
findings.source: 4.3 Urban Configurational Features and Wayfinding Behaviour: Space syntax
findings.quote: Kim (2001) concluded that cognitive maps drawn by people living in areas with what the analysis suggests is a high value of intelligibility are better representors of their surrounding environment

findings.consequent: Difficult wayfinding, increased need for directional signage
findings.source: 4.3 Urban Configurational Features and Wayfinding Behaviour: Space syntax
findings.quote: Their research confirmed the results of previous studies that the most segregated areas in the plan are the most difficult places for people to find their way so people need directional signage to solve their wayfinding problems in these locations.

findings.antecedent: Higher visual connectivity and spatial accessibility (of road segments)
findings.source: 4.3 Urban Configurational Features and Wayfinding Behaviour: Space syntax
findings.quote: Their findings implied that people prefer to choose road segments with higher values of visual connectivity and spatial accessibility.

synthesis_conclusions: The paper reviewed the main theory relating to spatial cognition and the creation of mental images of cities, in how individuals are perceiving and conceiving the urban environment.
Previous studies on the role of cognitive mapping and urban form in wayfinding behaviour of people were also examined.

Urban form characteristics, including Lynch's elements (paths, edges, nodes, districts, landmarks) and Weisman's variables (visual access, differentiation, layout configuration, signage), play an important role in wayfinding ability and performance.
Space syntax analysis (integration, connectivity, intelligibility) provides quantitative measures that correlate with pedestrian movement, route choice, and cognitive map formation.
Theories like Lynchian theory, urban semiotics, the flâneur concept, and space syntax offer different perspectives on how urban image is created and influences navigation.
evidence_gaps: How visitors make sense of an urban environment, create mental imagery, and then use that image to navigate the city.
How way-showing aids (paper maps, GPS devices, smartphone apps) affect mental image creation, and whether they complement or disrupt spatial knowledge acquisition processes.
The specific spatial problems that transport and planning agencies may wish to address regarding human navigation.
limitations: Previous work has limitations in overcoming conceptual and perceptual issues related to wayfinding.
Space syntax elements are not yet fully tested for their match with actual image creation in human wayfinders.
Space syntax struggles to encapsulate conceptual issues, as criticized by semiologists of Lynch's work.

theory_commitments.specific_claim: Urban environments can be understood and navigated more easily if they possess distinct elements (paths, edges, nodes, districts, landmarks) that contribute to their overall imageability and legibility.

mechanism_chain.description: The process by which distinct urban elements are perceived and integrated into a coherent mental representation, facilitating the understanding and navigation of an urban environment.

steps.from_construct: Urban elements (paths, edges, nodes, districts, landmarks)
steps.to_construct: Perception and recognition of distinct urban features

steps.from_construct: Perception and recognition of distinct urban features
steps.to_construct: Formation of a coherent cognitive map/mental representation (urban legibility and imageability)
